articles.title: Spain and Greece refuse to transfer Patriot systems to Ukraine whose service life is nearing its end - media
articles.body:
Spain and Greece refuse to transfer Patriot systems to Ukraine whose service life is nearing its end - media
Kyiv • UNN
Greece and Spain have Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose service life is expiring. NATO and the EU are calling on them to transfer them to Ukraine.
Greece and Spain possess stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems whose expiration dates are approaching. These missiles could be transferred to Ukraine, but the countries have so far refused, reports UNN, citing The Telegraph.
The publication notes that Greece and Spain— two NATO countries—have some of the largest stocks of such missiles in Europe, while Kyiv is persistently asking for additional means of protection against Russia's plans to carry out the most severe long-range mass strikes of the war.
Ukrainian officials have disclosed information about intercepted Russian plans for a new campaign aimed at destroying the country's energy system, with the goal of plunging cities into darkness and testing the population's resilience during the winter period.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly called on allies to provide more interceptor missiles for the American Patriot systems currently in Ukraine—the most effective systems for shooting down enemy warheads.
Kyiv fears that Russian forces could use a thousand missiles, drones, and aerial bombs against electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, as well as the infrastructure of Ukraine's three operating nuclear power plants.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine needs between 300 and 360 Patriot interceptor missiles to withstand Russia's winter campaign.
Given the urgent need to provide Ukraine with the necessary means, efforts have focused on encouraging Greece and Spain to transfer part of their stocks.
NATO and EU representatives have tried to persuade Greece and Spain to transfer Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles to Ukraine whose expiration dates are approaching.
Greece is believed to have at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles, whose service life—calculated at 23 years—will soon expire.
The exact number of missiles in Spain's reserve is unknown, although last month the country's foreign minister announced that Madrid would transfer five interceptors to Kyiv.
Participants in the talks are reluctant to name the two countries publicly, fearing that this could damage relations with them.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas raised the issue during talks in Ireland last month, stating: "We know that some countries have interceptor missiles whose expiration dates will soon pass. So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine."
As a diplomatic source told The Telegraph, the approach chosen is to ask Greece and Spain: "How can we help you make this decision?"
"It would be logical if at least those interceptor missiles whose expiration dates are approaching were sent to Ukraine," the interlocutor added.
Interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, like other missiles, have a specified storage life during which the manufacturer guarantees their effectiveness.
Fabian Hoffmann, a missile-weapons expert from the University of Oslo, said: "The manufacturer guarantees that the missile will function properly for a certain period of time. After this period ends, the missiles must undergo recertification.
During recertification, components whose expiration dates have passed—such as batteries or rocket engines—are replaced, and the operability of the remaining systems is also checked.
Of course, missiles may function even after their expiration date, but if they fail, the manufacturer bears no responsibility for this."
Ukraine receives 95% of its Patriot missiles through a NATO-led initiative that involves using European funds to directly purchase these interceptors from the United States.
However, the war with Iran has caused a global shortage that even Washington is finding difficult to overcome.
According to some estimates, the United States and its allies used at least 800 Patriot interceptor missiles in the first days of the conflict that erupted in February.
At the time, senior Ukrainian officials said that Kyiv had received only 600 such missiles over four years.
Earlier this year, the Ukrainian Air Force stopped publishing daily data on the number of intercepted ballistic missiles amid an increasingly acute shortage of ammunition.
Anonymous sources cited by The New York Times suggest that the U.S. stockpile of Patriot missiles may total fewer than 1,700 units.
This raised questions about the Pentagon's readiness to replenish Ukraine's supplies at a time when the United States itself is engaged in hostilities against Iran.
The Telegraph approached the defense ministries of Greece and Spain for comment.

articles.title: Three days of strikes, five Trump vetoes: Pentagon prepares for Iran war
articles.body:
The Pentagon has developed plans for a short but intensive military campaign against Iran, potentially lasting just three days and targeting its missile and drone arsenals, energy infrastructure and command centers. Yet despite the growing American military buildup in the Middle East, President Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to authorize a major new offensive, even as Iranian attacks on commercial shipping intensify.
The New York Times reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials, that Trump's national security team and the Pentagon have presented him with five proposals for significant military operations against Iran or the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen in recent months. He rejected all five, although he has once again instructed military planners to prepare options for renewed strikes.
On Thursday, Trump announced on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, adding that Washington and Tehran were “having productive discussions.”
The announcement came as American forces continued assembling one of their largest naval deployments to the Middle East in more than two decades, with three aircraft carriers expected to operate in the region by late October.
Despite the preparations, senior administration officials remain divided over whether another military campaign would achieve meaningful results, particularly as Iran has improved its military capabilities and American commanders warn of mounting pressure on U.S. missile defense stockpiles.
A three-day campaign targeting Iran's military infrastructure
The latest military planning was discussed last Friday at Camp David during a meeting of senior national security officials led by Vice President JD Vance.
The central proposal involves a concentrated campaign lasting approximately three days, intended to inflict significant damage on Iran's military capabilities without necessarily committing the United States to another prolonged conflict.
The potential targets include ballistic missile launchers and stockpiles, drone infrastructure and military facilities associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Energy installations and Revolutionary Guard headquarters and command posts are also under consideration.
American officials believe that Iran has rebuilt substantial portions of its missile and drone arsenal since the initial stages of the war, restoring capabilities that had previously been damaged.
Although Trump has ordered the preparation of updated military options, officials say his reluctance to resume large-scale combat has become increasingly apparent.
During the summer, American forces regularly carried out retaliatory attacks following Iranian strikes on international shipping. In recent weeks, however, Washington's response has become considerably more restrained.
The United States has continued operations against Iranian drones and cruise missiles but has refrained from launching major new strikes inside Iranian territory or attacking the country's shadow fleet of oil tankers.
Some members of Trump's inner circle have also become increasingly skeptical that another round of military action would persuade Tehran to change its position.
They argue that Washington's campaign of economic pressure is beginning to produce results and that additional time could force the Iranian leadership to make concessions without renewed large-scale fighting.
Other officials favor a more forceful approach, arguing that Iran's weakening economy could make it particularly vulnerable to a concentrated military campaign, especially one that undermines its ability to control maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Three aircraft carriers, 20,000 personnel and hundreds of aircraft
As the White House weighs its options, the American military is assembling a force capable of launching major operations against Iran on short notice.
The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt, which departed San Diego last week, is expected to join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington in the Middle East around the end of October.
The deployment would mark the first time since 2003, the year of the U.S. invasion of Iraq, that three American aircraft carriers have operated in the region simultaneously.
Each carrier strike group includes additional warships and supporting military assets, significantly expanding the range of offensive and defensive capabilities available to American commanders.
By the end of October, more than 20,000 sailors and Marines are expected to be deployed aboard vessels in the region, alongside hundreds of military aircraft.
The unusually large concentration of forces is not expected to last long. The George Washington is scheduled to return to its base in Japan after the Theodore Roosevelt arrives to replace it.
Military commanders are nevertheless prepared to launch a major operation within days if Trump reverses his position and authorizes renewed strikes.
The scale of the buildup has not resolved concerns about the potential consequences of another confrontation.
Senior defense officials are particularly worried that a new campaign could further deplete American stocks of defensive munitions, which have already come under considerable pressure during the conflict.
The United States must maintain enough interceptors to protect its forces in the Middle East while preserving defensive capabilities for other potential crises around the world.
Iran's military tactics have become more difficult to counter
One of the major complications facing American military planners is the improvement in Iran's ability to carry out attacks against U.S. forces and regional infrastructure.
Iranian forces have adjusted their tactics during the war, making missile attacks increasingly difficult to intercept and forcing American defense systems to expend more ammunition.
During the early stages of the conflict, U.S. forces generally launched two interceptors at incoming Iranian missiles, concentrating their defensive efforts on the most threatening attacks.
More recently, neutralizing Iranian missile salvos has required a greater number of interceptors, creating additional strain on supplies that are already stretched.
American intelligence assessments have also identified another challenge: Iranian forces have gained access to satellite imagery supplied by Chinese companies, improving their ability to identify and target American military installations.
People familiar with the intelligence assessments say the imagery has helped Iran conduct more effective attacks against U.S. bases.
American commanders are increasingly concerned about their ability to defend military installations housing U.S. personnel, as well as energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure across the region.
A renewed offensive could trigger additional Iranian retaliation, requiring even more defensive missiles at a time when the American military is attempting to preserve its remaining inventory.
The concerns have become an important factor in the debate over whether the benefits of another military operation would outweigh the risks.
Nearly 20 ships targeted as tensions rise in the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has continued to target commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters, adding to concerns about the security of one of the world's most important energy transportation routes.
Since September, when the last major exchange of retaliatory strikes took place, Iran has attacked at least 13 vessels, according to a maritime monitoring group operated by the British Navy.
Intelligence assessments suggest the actual number could be closer to 20.
Despite the attacks, none has triggered a major American military response.
The increasingly restrained U.S. reaction marks a change from the summer, when Washington routinely retaliated against Iranian attacks on international shipping.
Although oil exports from the Middle East have increased, the continuing attacks have unsettled shipping companies and raised concerns about the longer-term reliability of regional energy shipments.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of tension.
Trump claimed Thursday that none of the oil passing through the strait originated in Iran, but intelligence assessments indicate that the situation is more complicated.
Iran continues to permit certain vessels to transit the waterway, including ships that have paid passage fees and others potentially carrying Iranian oil.
Chinese companies have paid Iran for passage through the strait, while Tehran also operates a shadow fleet of tankers used to transport oil despite international sanctions.
Iran has additionally been accused of secretly blending its crude oil with Iraqi oil to disguise its origin and circumvent sanctions.
On Thursday, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions against 17 vessels it identified as part of Iran's shadow fleet involved in oil smuggling.
The combination of maritime attacks, sanctions enforcement and uncertainty over future military operations has placed additional pressure on commercial shipping through the region.
Nuclear talks remain stalled as elections approach
Alongside the military preparations, diplomatic contacts between Washington and Tehran have continued through intermediaries.
American officials acknowledge that some progress has been made, but negotiations remain stalled over the sequencing of discussions about Iran's nuclear program.
Washington wants an agreement addressing Tehran's nuclear ambitions to come first, while Iranian negotiators insist that the nuclear issue should be left until the final stage of negotiations.
The disagreement has prevented the two sides from reaching a broader understanding, even as Trump maintains that diplomatic discussions remain productive.
The approaching elections in Israel and the United States have also influenced the administration's calculations.
Before Trump's public commitment not to attack Iran ahead of the U.S. midterms, American officials had already anticipated that he might postpone a decision until after Israel's parliamentary elections on October 27 and the American vote the following week.
The political timetable would allow the administration to assess its military and diplomatic options without launching another major conflict immediately before voters head to the polls.
Yet even after the elections, there is no certainty that Trump will authorize renewed attacks.
The president has repeatedly rejected military proposals despite pressure from some officials who favor a more aggressive response to Iran's actions.
Military commanders, meanwhile, continue preparing for the possibility that the administration will abruptly change course.
Supporters of additional strikes believe a short, intense campaign could exploit Iran's deteriorating economic situation and further weaken its military capabilities, particularly if it limits Tehran's ability to influence shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Others fear that renewed combat would produce another cycle of Iranian retaliation, increase the burden on American missile defenses and fail to resolve the underlying dispute over Iran's nuclear program.
For now, the United States is positioning enough military power in the Middle East to launch a major offensive while its president continues to favor delaying the decision.
With three aircraft carriers moving toward the region and operational plans already prepared, the central question is no longer whether the American military can launch another attack against Iran, but whether Trump will ultimately authorize one.

articles.title: EXPLAINER - How has Russia-Ukraine fighting intensified since September?
articles.body:
- Russia and Ukraine claim that targeting of infrastructure is linked to military and military-related activities while countries accuse each other of endangering or killing civilians
- Tensions extend beyond Ukraine, with Russia’s westernmost exclave of Kaliningrad adding to friction between Moscow and Europe
Fighting between Russia and Ukraine has intensified since early last month, with attacks increasing in both frequency and scope.
Russia has stepped up attacks targeting Ukraine’s railways, bridges, port infrastructure, electricity facilities and transport hubs, including sites close to the Polish border and in the capital Kyiv.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has intensified attacks deep inside Russia, hitting oil refineries and fuel infrastructure as well as military airfields and air-defense systems.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.
Amid the surge in strikes, tensions between Russia and NATO have also increased, particularly around the Baltic Sea, with Moscow warning NATO that Russia was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance attempted to isolate its westernmost exclave of Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Russian strikes in Ukraine
Since early September, Russian strikes in Ukraine have killed and injured many people while also damaging local infrastructure in multiple regions, according to reports, including by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
Among the reported targets of such strikes were a border checkpoint with Romania on Sept. 6 as well as the building of the My-Ukraina TV channel, part of the country’s United News telethon, on Sept. 8.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of carrying out “demonstrative strikes” on airports near the country's capital ahead of a planned visit to Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The Sept. 6 trip marked Witkoff and Kushner's first visit to Ukraine since US-mediated peace negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv began.
Apart from Kyiv, other Ukrainian regions have also been the target of Russian airstrikes, most notably the southern region of Odesa, where infrastructure and vessels approaching Ukrainian ports have been hit.
On Sept. 12, Ukrainian authorities said at least 48 people were injured following Russian strikes in the region, which Zelenskyy said also hit a hotel in the port city of Chornomorsk.
The Russian Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed it hit port infrastructure facilities at the port of Chornomorsk that were “used for unloading and storing military supplies” as well as two dry-cargo vessels and a sea tugboat during overnight strikes.
Railway infrastructure has also been targeted by Russian strikes, with one of the most notable incidents occurring on Sept. 14, when a Warsaw-bound train was hit by a drone near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the Volyn region.
Ukraine claimed that the Russian drone was likely targeting a diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European officials which had left the station before the strike.
Moscow said later that day it was continuing to target railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that were “used for transporting military cargo from European countries.”
Ukrainian strikes in Russia
During the same period, Russia reported extensively on Ukrainian strikes, particularly targeting the energy sector.
Local authorities reported continued strikes on Russian logistics centers, including on Sept. 11, when a drone attack hit facilities belonging to online retailer Ozon.
Ukraine has intensified drone strikes on Russian logistics facilities in a campaign that began in mid-July and has spread across several Russian regions.
Since July, Ukrainian drones have targeted logistics centers of Russia's largest e-commerce retailer Wildberries in multiple regions, and strikes have expanded to facilities belonging to Ozon since August.
Kyiv has alleged that both retailers are playing a role in Russia’s military supply chain, while Moscow and the two companies maintain that the facilities are commercial.
Ukrainian strikes have also continued to target energy facilities across several Russian regions, including the Novorossiysk oil terminal in the southern Krasnodar region and facilities at the port of Ust-Luga in the northwestern Leningrad region.
The sustained attacks have constrained Russia's ability to process crude into transportation fuels. In response, Russia introduced diesel export curbs in July and extended them through September.
US President Donald Trump urged Zelenskyy in mid-September to halt military strikes against Russian diesel refineries, warning that the operations are creating global fuel shortages.
Russia also accused Ukraine of attempting to disrupt its Sept. 18-20 parliamentary elections, during which it said Kyiv targeted local infrastructure, including polling stations. Ukraine did not comment on the accusation.
Kaliningrad tensions
The escalation amid the ongoing war in Ukraine has also become increasingly visible beyond the war-torn country due to rhetoric surrounding Russia's Kaliningrad region.
A Russian semi-exclave bordered by Lithuania to the north and east, Poland to the south, and the Baltic Sea to the west and northwest, the Kaliningrad region has captured media attention after some Russian diplomatic missions in Europe warned that Moscow would use "all weapons" in its arsenal to defend its territory, including nuclear arms.
"Those advocating plans to blockade or strike Kaliningrad should have no illusions about the consequences. Any British or NATO military action against Russian territory would be met with a response using all means at Russia’s disposal, including nuclear weapons," the Russian Embassy in the UK said on Sept. 29.
At a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin also said that any direct attack on Russia or attempt to annex the exclave would inevitably raise the issue of using "all weapons and means at Moscow’s disposal."
Putin's remarks came after reports that Russia had sent a letter to NATO reiterating Moscow's position concerning the Kaliningrad region.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte did not disclose the contents of the letter but told journalists on Sept. 30 that the organization had responded.
“We are a defensive alliance,” he said, calling on Russia to "stop the nuclear threats" and “stop the war in Ukraine.”

articles.title: British nuclear subs have only fire hoses as drone defense – media
articles.body:
British nuclear subs have only fire hoses as drone defense – media
British sailors are drilling to fend off potential drone attacks against £4 billion ($5.3 billion) Vanguard-class subs using fire hoses as the only onboard “air defense weapon,” The Sun has reported.
The hoses, known as “center fed reels” are placed on submarine decks as a precaution when the vessels are moored at the British naval base Clyde in Scotland, the UK’s most sensitive military site, the tabloid reported on Thursday, citing anonymous sources. The equipment has pistol-grip nozzles that would allow sailors to direct water at approaching drones.
“You have to use what you’ve got,” the tabloid cited one of its sources as saying.
The Royal Navy’s four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines are the only British platforms equipped to carry and launch Trident II nuclear missiles, which deliver the UK’s only operational nuclear weapons. According to The Sun, the Navy insists that layered defenses, including “physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone capabilities,” protect the subs.
The report comes as the Royal Navy is facing what a former senior commander has described as its worst crisis in 350 years.
The UK’s entire fleet of nuclear-powered Astute-class attack submarines are not fit for combat duty, retired chief of the Naval Staff, Lord Alan West, told The Sun earlier this year. Five of the vessels are facing maintenance and availability delays, while the sixth, according to the Royal Navy, is still undergoing sea trials ahead of returning to service.
West described the number of ships the Navy has as “pathetic.” The fleet has just five operational frigates and no amphibious assault ships, while former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government retired four frigates, two assault ships, two tankers, and a nuclear-powered submarine during his time in office, The Sun reported in July.
This year, the UK has pledged an additional £15 billion in military funding, citing alleged threats from Russia. London has also seized and aided in seizing ships it has accused of being part of the so-called Russian ‘shadow fleet’ – a practice Moscow has denounced as “piracy.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Moscow wants to attack NATO and has accused Western European leaders of escalating tensions with Moscow, pointing to their statements about preparing for a possible war with Russia in 2029 or 2030, repeated military exercises in the Baltic Sea, and attempts to detain Russian vessels. “This is all escalation,” he said last week.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Drones strike another Yandex data center in Russia
articles.body:
Key developments on October 09:
- Second Russian Yandex data center damaged by drone attack in two days, company says
- Twenty Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on Donetsk, independent monitors claim
- Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
- Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
- Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities
A drone attack damaged a Yandex data center in Russia's Kaluga Oblast overnight on Oct. 9, disabling several modules at the facility and threatening further disruptions to the company's services.
Several modules of the data center were completely disabled, Yandex said in a statement carried by pro-government Russian newspaper Vedomosti.
"Some Yandex services may experience disruptions as a result," the company said, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Yandex reported no injuries at the facility.
The attack came as drones struck other parts of Kaluga Oblast overnight, injuring nine people, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He also reported damage to houses in two districts of the oblast. Russian authorities claimed to have shot down 26 drones over the region.
Ukraine has not publicly confirmed responsibility for the attack on the Kaluga data center.
The strike marks the second reported attack on a Yandex data center in Russia in two days.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at a major Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing the facility to suspend operations and disrupting parts of Yandex's cloud infrastructure.
The Sasovo facility houses tens of thousands of servers and two of the company's three supercomputers used to develop artificial intelligence models. Yandex said it was still assessing whether damaged equipment could be restored.
The attack coincided with reports of widespread internet disruptions across Russia, affecting banking services, transport websites, and online platforms.
Responding to questions about the Sasovo strike on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would continue retaliating against Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
"We responded to them," he added. "I cannot share all the details."
Russian forces struck several Ukrainian internet providers and data centers in Kyiv in late September, disrupting internet access for approximately 100,000 households, according to Ukrainian officials.
read also
Record 20 Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on headquarters in Donetsk, monitors say
Ukrainian missile strikes on Russian army command posts in Donetsk on Aug. 26 killed more Russian officers than in any other single attack during the war, independent monitors claim.
Mediazona, an independent Russian outlet that tracks Russian military deaths in collaboration with the BBC Russian Service, identified 20 officers killed in the attack.
Each of the dead Russian officers was identified by name, age, and rank by Mediazona. Seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain, and one senior lieutenant were killed in the strikes, which hit the headquarters of the Central Military District and the 41st Combined Arms Army in occupied Donetsk.
According to Mediazona, 18 of the Russian officers died immediately in the missile strike, while two succumbed to their injuries.
Denis Pushilin, the head of the Russian illegal occupation administration in Donetsk Oblast, confirmed in a post on Telegram that Ukraine had launched an attack on targets in Donetsk on Aug. 26, claiming that Anglo-French "Storm Shadow" air-launched cruise missiles were used, and that eight civilians were injured.
Mediazona also identified two other instances of "mass casualties" amongst staff officers of the 41st Combined Arms Army, according to their research, eight officers were killed on Aug. 4, with an additional four killed on Sept 8, 2025.
At least 276,113 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine since 2022, according to Mediazona, which tracks individuals killed by searching through obituaries, posts on Russian social media networks, and leaked Russian databases.
read also
Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
Russian forces forcibly removed 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territory in Kharkiv Oblast to an unknown destination, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 9.
The civilians, including children, young people, and elderly residents, were taken from an area of the oblast where active fighting continues. Their current whereabouts and the conditions in which they are being held remain unknown, Lubinets said.
"Russia calls this an 'evacuation.' But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated, and left with no choice, it is not a rescue. It is coercion," Lubinets said.
The ombudsman did not specify which settlement the civilians were taken from or where they had been transported.
According to Lubinets, Russian forces published footage of what they described as a rescue operation on their Telegram channels. He said the footage showed signs of intimidation and pressure on civilians who had not consented to being relocated.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the circumstances of the reported removals.
Lubinets also warned that Russian occupation authorities had created a Telegram bot to collect personal information under the pretext of evacuation, potentially putting civilians and their relatives at risk.
Forcible transfers and deportations of civilians from occupied territory are prohibited under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Lubinets said he had appealed to Russia's human rights commissioner, demanding information about the 25 civilians, their whereabouts and conditions, and measures to secure their return to Ukraine.
He also appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the United Nations, and other international organizations for assistance.
Russia has repeatedly forcibly transferred and deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territories since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In March 2026, a United Nations commission concluded that Russia's deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children amounted to crimes against humanity.
read also
Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
Several Moscow airports temporarily suspended flights on Oct. 9, as suspected Ukrainian drones and balloons entered airspace around the Russian capital.
Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports all halted operations during the alleged Ukrainian raid, disrupting flights and causing long delays.
According to FlightRadar24, an open-source air traffic monitoring website, multiple Russian government aircraft from the Rossiya Special Flight Detachment, which transports top-level Russian government officials, were scheduled to fly into Moscow's airports on Oct. 9.
At least one of the aircraft, an Ilyushin Il-96-300PU flying from Türkmenbaşy in Turkmenistan to Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, was reportedly forced to divert to St. Petersburg, according to FlightRadar24.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed "the Ministry of Defense's air defense forces repelled an attack by 15 UAVs" on the Russian government's messaging app, MAX.
A number of unknown balloons, which both Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels claimed were launched by the Ukrainian military, were also seen in the Russian skies.
Local Russian Telegram channels showed mysterious balloons in the skies near Moscow, and air defense activity.
Russian outlet BAZA claimed that, "reconnaissance balloons launched from Ukraine," were shot down over Yaroslavl Oblast, a region of Russia north of Moscow.
By 5:42 p.m. Moscow time, Russian wire service RIA Novosti reported that Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports had reopened.
On Sept. 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced a plan to close Russia's skies.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said, as he warned "every airline that uses Russian airspace" against flying over the country.
"The Russian sky will be de facto closed," he added.
In the weeks following the announcement, Ukrainian drone raids have caused severe disruption to Russian air travel, but the result has fallen short of the complete closure Zelensky promised.
read also
Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said.
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+, citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said.
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

articles.title: US Congress Delegation Backs Expanded Starlink Access for Ukraine
articles.body:
A delegation of US lawmakers has backed expanding Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network and urged an effort to win over the company’s owner, Elon Musk, who has repeatedly refused to allow its use inside Russia over fears of nuclear escalation.
US Representative Dan Crenshaw, a Texas Republican, made the remarks during the delegation’s visit to Kyiv on Friday, Oct. 9, according to Ukrinform.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The delegation also included Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Sens. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota and Markwayne Mullin of Oklahoma, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky’s statement issued later on Friday.
“I will say in my own name, but I think the others present will agree with me: I fully support the idea of trying to convince Elon Musk to activate Starlink,” Crenshaw said.
Three other members of the delegation also voiced their agreement, Ukrinform reported.
‘Leverage’ over Moscow
Crenshaw reportedly argued that wider Starlink use, along with the sweeping sanctions championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, would give Washington more leverage over Russia.
Addressing Musk directly, Crenshaw acknowledged the billionaire’s fear of escalation, while adding that sometimes the escalation is unavoidable and, at times, even necessary to reduce further tensions.
Senator Roger Wicker, the Mississippi Republican who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he hoped an agreement could be reached with Musk, according to Ukrinform.
Sybiha Presses WTO Chief on Black Sea Shipping, Remote Audits
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran was signed into law on Sept. 18 by US President Donald Trump. The law essentially gave the White House authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Altogether, the bill is aimed at cutting Russia’s war revenues; it targets Russian President Vladimir Putin and other senior diplomats closely connected to the Kremlin, Moscow’s defense sectors and financial institutions.
Other networks helping Moscow evade existing sanctions and conduct the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children can also be sanctioned. However, the authority to impose sanctions on Russia does not automatically mean that the president will use it.
Zelensky presses for sanctions, Patriot production
During the entire duration of their meeting, an air-raid alert over the threat of jet-powered Shahed drones stayed in effect, Zelensky said, thanking the US lawmakers for standing with Ukrainians amid near-constant Russian attacks.
The President briefed the delegation on Russian drone attacks which damaged two schools in Kyiv alone since the start of October.
Bridges, energy facilities and other critical infrastructure sustained damage as well, he said, arguing that Russia is escalating its attacks to make up for failing to achieve its goals on the battlefield.
“This terror can be countered only together, and we discussed how the United States can help save lives,” Zelensky said, adding that Kyiv expects the US to implement the Graham sanctions law.
“This is a matter of political will, and it is now important to demonstrate leadership and fully restrict financial flows to Russia’s war machine,” he continued.
Speeding up licensing for Patriot missile production in Ukraine was also on the agenda.
Trump had agreed to grant Kyiv the license to produce its own interceptors domestically during his meeting with Zelensky on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, late September.
The US president initially announced the license transfer in July but later backtracked on the commitment, saying Washington must exercise caution when sharing sensitive military technology.
“Ukraine is ready not only to produce ballistic-missile interceptors for itself, but also to strengthen the United States and its allies through joint production,” Zelensky said.
Kyiv’s consistent push to use Starlink inside Russia
Currently, SpaceX allows Ukraine to use Starlink on Ukrainian-controlled territory, including Russian-occupied areas such as Crimea. However, the service inside Russia is completely blocked.
Because of this, Ukraine’s long-range drones rely on alternative navigation systems, including AI-based technology, when conducting strikes across its border.
Kyiv had asked Washington to help secure permission to use Starlink on drones targeting Russian ballistic missile launchers up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) inside Russia, according to Financial Times on Aug. 21.
Zelensky reportedly raised the issue with Trump during a late-July meeting at the White House. Although Trump said he would consider the request, he made no tangible commitment to support it.
Allowing Ukraine to use Starlink could ease pressure on the country’s already critically limited stock of Patriot missile interceptors.
According to FT, Zelensky argued that it could also improve targeting that is needed to down Russia’s ballistic missile launchers ahead of winter, when Moscow is expected to intensify its campaign against critical Ukrainian infrastructure.
Ukraine was still negotiating with the US over using Starlink on Russian territory for defense purposes in late August, Ukrinform reported citing Zelensky.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1688: Russian strike on two passenger buses kills 30 in Kramatorsk
articles.body:
Military
Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant. In Bashkortostan, Ukraine’s General Staff says its forces hit a Gazprom refinery. Salavat’s mayor says an unnamed enterprise there keeps working.
Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says. The faster drones break through Ukraine’s air defenses more reliably, and ISW expects the same strike pattern in Russia’s winter campaign against Ukraine’s energy.
Kalashnikov, Russia’s biggest small-arms maker, says it fills its entire 2026 arms contract on time with batch of 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifle. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said in February that nearly half of Kalashnikov’s plants faced no sanctions from any coalition country.
Ukraine says it struck plant making parts for Russian military aircraft engines—a Snizhne factory Russia has used since 2014. Ukraine’s 413th Raid Regiment has released footage showing the strike on a facility that produces components for gas-turbine engines used in attack aircraft and combat helicopters.
Intelligence and technology
Sea drone vs. air drone: Ukraine’s Sargan-3000 turns anti-aircraft gunner. A radio-steered Russian Shahed met a remote-controlled machine gun at sea—operator against operator, and the gun won.
Ukraine’s Frodo robot carries wounded soldier in first reported evacuation. The mission involved one of the first Frodo versions supplied to the military for testing, according to its developer.
It was built to shield Russian crops from hail. Now it’s being pitched as a drone interceptor. In farm service, the Alazan flies about 10 km and climbs up to 8 km. Russian state TV showed a guided version at a training range Putin toured.
AI is changing Russia’s drone war on Ukrainian cities, deputy air defense commander says. Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 drones carry machine vision that lets them recognize and track targets.
Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones. The hybrid has already downed about 20 air targets.
International
Moldova pulls its border officers off Ukrainian soil again as Russian drones keep hitting crossings. “They will work on the territory of Moldova.” Moldovan Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin, on withdrawing border personnel from Ukraine.
Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization. The move comes as Moscow rejects reports of a new call-up while Ukrainian officials warn Russia is preparing to expand its forces.
80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership. A new poll shows widespread concern over Moldova’s ability to withstand an attack, even as only 4% of respondents see NATO membership as the answer. Russian drones have increasingly crossed Moldovan airspace in recent weeks.
Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion. More than 30 Russian drones entered Polish airspace in September 2025, and some were found carrying Polish SIM cards, RMF24 reports.
German radar already guarding Ukraine is picked to spot ballistic missiles. Its maker just signed a new deal with Kyiv. Hensoldt and Kyiv will also study jointly operating a bigger radar, the TRL-4D LR, whose naval version reaches beyond 400 km.
Ukrainian drugmakers sold $114 million worth of medicines to Uzbekistan in six months. Now they may lose the right to sell there. That export cash keeps medicine prices low at home. Without it, drugs could get pricier for Ukrainian patients, a former regulator official says.
First time since 2018: NATO’s top military body went to Kyiv to study the war it may one day face. Military representatives of all 32 members heard the latest battlefield assessment from Ukraine’s command.
Humanitarian and social impact
Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter. Russia is once again targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as winter approaches, threatening to leave civilians without power, heat, and water as Moscow ramps up its campaign to cripple the country’s critical systems.
Two 14-year-old boys killed by an explosive device in a field in Sumy Oblast. Residents are being warned that, in addition to constant Russian attacks, there is a risk of encountering explosive devices.
Russia kills 30 in strike on two passenger buses in Kramatorsk. Hours after the strike, the head of Donetsk Oblast ordered public transport in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk halted, saying Russia had made the buses a target.
A 3-year-old girl came to visit her aunt in Pryluky, Ukraine. By morning, a Russian missile had killed her grandmother and uncle. Zlatoslava is in hospital in Chernihiv. Her aunt, a police officer, was wounded in the strike.
22 killed in Russian missile strike on Pryluky, including five children. Rescuers have finished searching the rubble of the five-story apartment building a Russian missile hit yesterday morning, while residents were still asleep.
Ukraine is buying 135 mobile shelters for border crossings as Russian drones reach from the Danube to Poland. Regional recovery services have opened 10 tenders, one of them for shelters on the road to a crossing into Romania.
Oleksandr, Kyrylo and Serhii, all aged one, and eight-year-old Maksym were killed in Ukraine’s city by Russian strike on Putin’s birthday. A Russian missile flattened an apartment block in Pryluky.
Russia’s war on Ukrainian books: a second strike burns tens of thousands of a Kyiv publisher’s rebuilt titles. Knyholav lost new titles and reprints of books Russia had already burned in July.
Political and legal developments
Ukraine’s FM links Russian plague scare to history of cover-ups, from anthrax to Chornobyl and COVID-19. Russia’s handling of the suspected case fits a broader pattern of concealing information about dangerous incidents, Andrii Sybiha said.
Russia starts pouring more into war after Putin judged Alaska talks with US would bring no “acceptable” deal to end fighting — Bloomberg. Russia’s 2026 budget deficit has nearly doubled to more than $81 billion, as war spending blows past the original plan.
Russia’s war against Ukraine sends the bill to its own companies: bond defaults head for a 17-year high. The squeeze is spreading from small firms to Moscow’s own budget, which is running a record deficit to keep the war going.

articles.title: Zelenskyy blasts US over Russia ties as strikes kill 78 in Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of being unwilling to help Ukraine after Russian strikes killed 78 people and wounded 215 across the country in two days, urging President Donald Trump to increase military support and sanctions against Moscow.
The attacks included a devastating strike on the eastern city of Kramatorsk, where at least 35 people were killed and 20 wounded, according to Ukrainian officials.
The bombardment followed a major Russian drone and missile assault a day earlier that killed dozens, including 22 people in a residential building in Pryluky, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Speaking to reporters Thursday in Pryluky, Zelenskyy criticized Washington for pursuing potential economic cooperation with Russia while attempting to mediate the war, now in its fifth year.
He also called on the United States to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite communications network, saying it could help Ukrainian forces identify and target Russian ballistic missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran," Zelenskyy said. "Give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table."
The Ukrainian leader questioned U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assessment earlier Thursday that the war had reached a stalemate and Washington would continue working toward a settlement.
Zelenskyy argued that Washington's pursuit of economic projects with Moscow contradicted claims that diplomatic progress had stalled.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," he added.
His remarks followed a Reuters report that senior Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream pipeline network, which transported Russian natural gas to Germany before Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelenskyy urged Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia, arguing that stronger support for Ukraine could help bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table.
Ukrainian negotiators are scheduled to travel to the United States on Friday and Saturday for talks. Zelenskyy said he expected European partners to join the discussions, with air defense expected to be a key issue amid continued Russian attacks.
In Kramatorsk, a Russian guided aerial bomb struck the city Thursday, killing dozens and damaging two buses. A subsequent drone attack killed two more people, bringing the reported death toll to 35.
Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting civilians.
"The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible," he said on Telegram.
Images released by officials showed bodies scattered across a debris-covered street beside a charred bus. Some victims had not been identified, Zelenskyy said, warning that the attack would not go unanswered.
Elsewhere, a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region, while another person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk, local authorities said.
The latest bombardment followed Wednesday's attacks, which killed dozens across Ukraine, including 22 people in Pryluky.
Russia also attacked Kyiv on Thursday morning, killing four people and wounding 19, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The strikes disrupted water and electricity supplies in parts of the capital, with officials warning that restoring services would take time.
Moscow has intensified drone attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses, data centers and other infrastructure while renewing its campaign against Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter.
Russian technology company Yandex said it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data center hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored.
Zelenskyy did not specifically address the strike on Yandex but said Ukraine was mirroring Russian attacks on data centers.
Ukraine has sought to regain the battlefield initiative as Russian territorial advances have slowed this year. However, Moscow's sustained air campaign continues to threaten civilians, critical infrastructure and the country's energy security.

articles.title: As Trump mulls new strikes on Iran, what options does he have?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
As Trump mulls new strikes on Iran, what options does he have?
Following renewed US troop movements into the Middle East, the US is reportedly gearing up for a new round of strikes on Iran after weeks of deliberations by President Donald Trump.
Trump has on several occasions stated that he would not launch new strikes until after the midterm elections, the latest being on Thursday, saying on Truth Social that discussions with Iran were "productive."
Yet, according to both The New York Times and Axios, Trump mulled the possibility of further strikes following a meeting with his national security staff in Camp David on 2 October. A final decision is set to occur within the next seven to 10 days, Israel's Channel 12 reported.
The New Arab explores if and how the US military will escalate tensions, and if Iran will retaliate.
What is now in the region?
As it stands, the US has around 50,000 troops and a host of assets in the region, including the 82nd Airborne Division, air defence systems, surveillance, refuelling and strike aircraft that it built up before and during the start of the Iran war.
This includes the USS George Washington aircraft carrier, involved in blockading Iran and escorting shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, and the USS Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, housing the 11th Marine Expeditionary Group.
In recent weeks, reports have shed light on new deployments, with some stating there will be between 9,000 and 10,000 troops, including the 13th Marine Expeditionary Group aboard the USS Makin Island, stationed alongside the USS Theodor Roosevelt, according to The Wall Street Journal.
This would maintain US carrier deployments to the region at two, following the withdrawal of the USS George H.W. Bush, which has since arrived in Thailand. It is unknown if the George Washington is also set to withdraw.
The US has also sent two additional Patriot missile batteries, used to shoot down incoming ballistic missiles, to prop up the dense web of systems already deployed and further protect Saudi and Qatari energy sites, according to Axios.
What are Trump's options?
According to Dr Andreas Krieg, Senior Lecturer in Defence Studies at King's College London, the deployments signal that the US "wants to restore escalation dominance without yet committing to another major war", with the troop and carrier deployments acting as both deterrence and preparation.
"The US is reinforcing air and missile defence, force protection, ISR [Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance], logistics and command capacity around Israel and the Gulf, while simultaneously giving Trump a much larger menu of strike options," he told The New Arab.
That menu has been reported on by The New York Times, with five plans drawn up focusing on a short, three-day campaign of intense strikes focusing on the drone and missile arsenal of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, their command posts and headquarters, alongside energy facilities.
Strikes on infrastructure are also expected to occur in the event of a US bombardment, and Israel is also expected to take part in an escalation, with Israeli media reporting that Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir is being briefed on US preparations.
The deployment of two carriers is a key aspect of this, with Krieg noting that it gives US military flexibility in any strike campaign against Iran, increasing sortie rates, allowing the US to enforce a blockade and protect shipping, and giving the US options to escalate the campaign targets.
"Trump wants Tehran to believe that rejecting American terms could now carry a much higher military cost," Krieg said, adding "but these deployments also expose the central weakness of the US position: every additional American asset placed in the Gulf creates another target Iran can threaten".
How could Iran respond?
Like in previous rounds of attacks on Iran by the US or Israel, Tehran is likely to retaliate.
Krieg told The New Arab that Iran would likely respond in two stages, the first being a focus on survivability, with the IRGC and military dispersing assets into hardened facilities, using decoys and decentralising command, to survive the initial strikes.
The second would see a horizontal escalation, targeting US bases and logistics hubs, pressuring Gulf infrastructure, and disrupting maritime traffic around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb through its Houthi allies.
"I think Tehran's calculation remains that the Gulf is America's vulnerability. Iran would aim to make any renewed US campaign immediately costly for Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and global energy markets," he said.
"Iran is likely to answer by making clear that such an escalation cannot be geographically contained inside Iran."
This was echoed by Ali Vaez, Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, who told The New Arab that "Iran cannot match the US militarily, so its strategy is to make escalation costly and geographically expansive."
"Its leverage lies in convincing Washington that any attack on Iran will reverberate across the region," he added.
"I fear that a high US casualty event might compel Trump to throw caution to the wind and go after Iran's infrastructure, which will result in Iran scorching the region," Vaez said.
Is this the same as the February attack?
Much of what is being debated is similar to what played out in February when the war began, with Andreas Kreig telling The New Arab, "There is a striking degree of repetition. The United States still essentially has the same coercive menu it had at the beginning of the war."
Those same escalation plans are part of the same "strategic calculus" employed by both sides, Kreig added, noting that the US is continuing to attempt to use military power to shorten the conflict, despite not being able to translate military power into political leverage, while Iran is playing for time.
"Unless one side changes that underlying logic, we are likely to keep seeing variations of the same escalation pattern rather than a genuinely new strategy," Krieg said.

articles.title: Trump rules out US strikes on Iran before midterms as US Treasury imposes new sanctions
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections, asserting that the two countries are having "productive" talks about ending the six-month-old war.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd."
The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump's domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November's election.
Some 60% of Americans - including one in four Republicans - disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living.
Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but he has not offered a detailed plan for exiting the war.
Proposals exchanged aimed at ending war, opening Strait of Hormuz
Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer.
Iran's state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make "meaningful" reductions in its enrichment capacity.
The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied.
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu, and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.

articles.title: Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites
articles.body:
Russia is planning a winter strike campaign involving up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting, among other facilities, electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, and boiler houses. The information is contained in a document that, according to sources cited by The New York Times, Ukraine's Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented as an intercepted Russian plan to destroy energy infrastructure systematically. The newspaper reported on 2 October.
Russia has been striking critical infrastructure across Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion. Such attacks have become particularly frequent ahead of and during winter. Ukraine's recent battlefield gains may have prompted Putin to reconsider his strategy and attempt to force Ukraine to surrender through winter strikes, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggest. Russia's reported plans to attack Ukraine's energy, water supply, and sewage systems could threaten the basic living conditions of millions of people. Such strikes could increase pressure on civilians and the Ukrainian economy while forcing the state to divert more resources to emergency infrastructure repairs instead of defense needs.
The New York Times was unable to verify the document's authenticity independently, but noted that it was written in Russian and dated August.
Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy
A representative of Ukraine's defense-industrial sector who has reviewed the document believes it is more of a calculation than a finalized Russian military operations plan, according to Schemes, an investigative journalism project by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), in a report published on 8 October.
60 targets: how Russia could attack Ukraine's critical infrastructure
The document outlines how many missiles, drones, and bombs Russia would need to deprive Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa of electricity, heating, water, and sewage services, Radio Liberty reported on 9 October. The document's full list of priority cities also includes Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia, and Ivano-Frankivsk.
According to the document, Russia plans to begin by attacking substations near Ukraine's western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe. Hydroelectric power plants could be targeted next, followed by facilities intended to shut down Ukraine's three operational nuclear power plants, Radio Liberty reports. The document lists a total of 60 key targets.
According to Schemes, the document states that Russia would need up to 770 Molniya and Geran drones, Dan-T/Banderol missile-drones, 170 FAB guided aerial bombs, and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles to carry out the attacks.
Sewage systems could become Russia's next target
The document devotes particular attention to water supply and wastewater systems. These include pumping stations, treatment facilities, and other infrastructure essential for cities to provide residents with water and dispose of wastewater.
Russia has not previously attacked such facilities on a similar scale, The New York Times notes.
Preparing for possible attacks on water supply and sewage systems is significantly more difficult than protecting energy infrastructure, Oleh Popenko, head of the Ukrainian Union of Utility Services Consumers, told Current Time, RFE/RL's Russian-language network.
“Sewage is a very complex system. There are specific challenges: where to discharge wastewater, how to organize treatment facilities, and so on. Some work is also underway in this sector, but it will be much more difficult here than with district heating utilities,” Popenko says.
Creating alternative routes in case sewage pumping stations are destroyed is an expensive and technically challenging task, he adds. Such construction could cost billions of hryvnias.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
The priority is to equip water utilities with backup power sources so they can continue operating during power outages. However, if Russian strikes damage the sewage system itself, resolving the problem quickly will be much more difficult, Popenko believes. Specific solutions, including wastewater disposal and the operation of treatment facilities, will have to be determined according to the extent of the damage.
Sewage pumping stations play a particularly important role. They pump wastewater onward for disposal and treatment. If such a station is put out of operation by a strike, the city needs an alternative way to divert wastewater while the damaged facility is being repaired, Popenko says. Bypass pipes or channels could be installed for this purpose, but setting up such a system during wartime is far from easy.
Air defenses remain crucial to Ukraine's winter preparations
Preparations for winter are underway, but protection for energy infrastructure remains inadequate, Popenko believes. The main concern is large substations that transmit electricity from nuclear power plants and distribute electricity imported from Europe.
At the same time, some protective measures are already proving effective. Despite drone attacks over two days, one of Kyiv's substations withstood the strikes, and the city did not lose power, although scheduled outages were in effect, the expert says.
Popenko considers a repeat of last winter's scenario, when parts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks, entirely possible. Russian forces continue to attack energy facilities, and in his assessment, strengthening air defenses in Kyiv is the only way to protect its combined heat and power (CHP) plants from large-scale attacks.
“There are no other ways — for example, building some sarcophagi around CHPs or constructing shelters — because Russia can destroy these facilities again through massive strikes. And then the city risks being left 50–60% without heat,” Popenko believes.
Residents are also preparing for winter, but their options vary, he says. Some homeowners' associations participate in government programs to insulate apartment buildings and purchase backup power supplies for elevators and pumping stations. Owners of private houses are buying generators, among other measures. However, such equipment and preparations require substantial funds, meaning not everyone can afford them, he notes.
Ukraine has already experienced prolonged power outages during previous winters, particularly in 2022 and 2023. At the time, some regions went without electricity for 18–20 hours a day, the expert says. This experience may help people prepare for possible disruptions, but it does not eliminate the risk of further attacks and infrastructure damage.
