articles.title: Iran questions France’s nuclear double standards
articles.body:
Iran questions France’s nuclear double standards
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei has criticized 'France’s contradictory approach' to nuclear weapons, questioning why Paris considers its own nuclear deterrent essential to national security while insisting that Iran must never possess nuclear weapons, despite Tehran’s stated commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
In a post on X, Baqaei contrasted French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks on the importance of military power and deterrence with his categorical opposition to Iran acquiring nuclear weapons.
During a test of a ballistic missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, Macron declared: “To be free, therefore, one must be feared, and to be feared, one must be powerful.”
Yet, as Baqaei noted, the French president has also insisted that Iran must never possess nuclear weapons, neither now nor in five or ten years.
The Iranian spokesperson argued that the central issue was not France’s possession of a nuclear deterrent, but the apparent double standard under which a rationale presented as essential to French security is treated as a threat when applied to Iran—even in discussions concerning a civilian nuclear program subject to international oversight.
Baqaei argued that the underlying problem was the desire of certain nuclear-armed powers to preserve their exclusive hold on strategic power and the authority to determine which countries may legitimately exercise it.
He said these powers seek to retain their own nuclear arsenals, presenting them as instruments of security and freedom, while invoking the prospect of a nuclear threat to justify restrictions on other countries, including those pursuing peaceful nuclear technology.
According to the Iranian diplomat, such an approach reflects a selective interpretation of security rather than a universal commitment to peace.
“A peace in which nuclear powers regard their own weapons as the guarantors of their freedom and security, but label the same logic a threat when invoked by others, is not true peace,” Baqaei wrote, arguing that this disparity amounted to a monopoly on power rooted in a sense of superiority.
Baqaei maintained that an international order that fails to recognize the equal right of all nations to security and peace risks reinforcing the dominance of a limited group of powerful states rather than safeguarding international stability.
His remarks placed the debate over Iran’s nuclear program within a broader question of consistency in international security policy: whether the principles invoked by nuclear-armed states to justify their own deterrence strategies should be applied fairly in their dealings with other countries.
Iran maintains that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes and has repeatedly called for its nuclear activities to be assessed on the basis of international law and safeguards obligations.
Baqaei’s criticism thus challenged France to reconcile its stated commitment to preventing nuclear proliferation with its own reliance on nuclear weapons as instruments of deterrence, arguing that lasting peace cannot be built on a system in which security is treated as a privilege reserved for a select group of powers.

articles.title: 52-year-old Russian political prisoner Igor Yakovenko dies in Krasnodar detention center after being returned for “palliative care”
articles.body:
Igor Yakovenko, a 52-year-old political prisoner, died in Krasnodar’s Pretrial Detention Center No. 1, according to a report by Memorial’s Support for Political Prisoners project. Yakovenko is at least the ninth political prisoner to die in Russian custody since the start of 2026, according to a count by The Insider. Human rights advocates said he had been diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor.
Several days before his death, Yakovenko underwent medical examinations and was then returned to the detention center “for palliative care.” Memorial also said Yakovenko had been beaten at the facility before he was sentenced.
On Oct. 3, 2025, the Southern District Military Court sentenced Yakovenko to five years in prison on charges of preparing to take part in the activities of a terrorist organization. Prosecutors alleged that on May 28, 2025, he began corresponding with a person involved in recruiting Russians for the Freedom of Russia Legion, which Russian authorities have designated a terrorist organization. Yakovenko allegedly planned to travel to Ukraine, sending the person a completed application form to join the Legion. FSB officers detained him two days later. Authorities did not disclose how they learned about the correspondence.
Memorial recognized Yakovenko as a political prisoner. The movement’s human rights advocates said they did not have access to the case files and therefore could not determine whether he genuinely intended to join the Legion or if had been the victim of an entrapment scheme. Memorial noted that only two days passed between Yakovenko sending the application and his arrest:
“Such a rapid sequence of events may indicate that from the outset he wrote to one of the Legion’s fake websites and sent his application there as well.”
In addition to Yakovenko, at least eight other political prisoners have died in Russian custody since the start of 2026:
- Roman Sidorkin died on Jan. 9 in the Saratov Region. The former employee of a defense company in the Kursk Region had been convicted of treason after investigators accused him and his former wife of passing technical documentation and samples of military products to Ukrainian intelligence. Sidorkin developed bronchitis-like symptoms in December 2025, and later pneumonia. He was hospitalized only four days before his death.
- Oleg Tyryshkin, a former miner and trade union activist from Kemerovo Region, died on Feb. 4 at age 64. He had been sentenced to two years in a penal colony over a comment posted on the social network VK about the 2004 death of Akhmat Kadyrov, the first president of Chechnya and the father of its current leader, Ramzan Kadyrov. Activists who corresponded with prisoners said heart problems were the cause of his death. Tyryshkin had previously complained about his health, including about a brain cyst.
- Alexander Dotsenko died on Feb. 19 after a massive heart attack. The jewelry artist had been sentenced to three years in a penal colony in a case involving anti-war postcards left in a Lenta supermarket in St. Petersburg. His wife, Anastasia Dyudyayeva, received a 3½-year sentence in the same case. After Dotsenko’s heart attack, prison officials failed to inform his relatives and lawyer about his condition for several days.
- Vladimir Osipov died in March at a pretrial detention center in Ukhta, where he had been transferred from the Moscow Region. The 56-year-old had been sentenced to 6½ years in a penal colony over posts made on Odnoklassniki about the Russian military and Vladimir Putin. Ambulances were called for Osipov several times during his trial, and at one hearing the judge refused to postpone his final statement despite complaints of high blood pressure.
- Andrei Akuzin, a 53-year-old artist from Komsomolsk-on-Amur, died by suicide on April 8 at a local pretrial detention center — six days after he was arrested. His friend said the criminal case stemmed from an online comment. Russia’s financial monitoring agency, Rosfinmonitoring, added Akuzin to its registry of “terrorists and extremists” only after his death.
- Vegan Khristolyub Bozhiy, formerly named Dmitry Kuznetsov, died on April 17 at Penal Colony No. 2 in Voronezh. The 43-year-old preacher and YouTube blogger, whose name can be loosely translated as “Vegan Christ-Lover of God,” had been sentenced to three years in prison over videos criticizing the invasion of Ukraine, the Soviet army, and Islam. It later emerged that he had been found hanged in a punishment cell and that, according to media reports, a negligence case was opened against the prison’s employees. His relatives did not believe the official account of suicide.
- Vladimir Yarotsky was found dead on the morning of May 7 at Penal Colony No. 9 in Khadyzhensk in Russia’s Krasnodar Region. The artist had been sentenced to five and a half years in prison on charges of spreading “false information” about the Russian armed forces and “desecrating symbols of military glory” over posts that included a caricature of Putin featuring a penis and a St. George ribbon. Authorities said Yarotsky died by suicide. Another prisoner said the artist had complained of pressure from the prison administration.
- Ibragim Kudzhanov, a 52-year-old resident of Ukraine’s Luhansk Region, died at Penal Colony No. 8 in the Omsk Region. His death became known in July. Kudzhanov had been sentenced to 5½ years in prison for serving as a driver in Ukraine’s Aidar Battalion in 2018 and 2019. His daughter said he had been tortured with electric shocks after his detention and that he died from a second heart attack accompanied by an aneurysm and kidney failure. His son, Artyom, is also imprisoned in Russia after being sentenced to 12 years in a penal colony on espionage charges in 2025.

articles.title: “Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare”: Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September, and winter will make it worse, analyst says
articles.body:
- Ukraine's "middle strikes" on Russian logistics haven't let up
- Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September
- A shift to protected convoys hasn't reduced the truck losses
Ukraine's campaign of so-called "middle strikes" targeting Russian supply lines isn't generating the same headlines it did back in the spring, when the campaign was intensifying.
But that doesn't mean Ukrainian units aren't launching thousands of drones a month and blowing up a lot of Russian trucks. Indeed, the pace of Ukrainian strikes, concentrated along the main supply routes threading through occupied southern Ukraine into occupied Crimea, has leveled off without ever really decreasing since an early summer surge.
It's evident Ukraine's middle-strike campaign "didn't stop and wasn't slowed down," noted French mapper Clément Molin, one of the most important observers of the counterlogistics campaign.
For September, Molin tallied 770 confirmed drone strikes on Russian trucks in the logistical zone 10 km beyond the line of contact. That's up from 630 strikes in August, 656 in July, and 586 in June, the month the campaign really got underway. There were just 214 strikes in May and at most a few dozen in each of the previous three months.
Whether Ukrainian troops can take advantage of the Russians' weakening logistics anytime soon is less evident.
Since June, the Ukrainians have hit around 700 Russian trucks a month that analysts can confirm with video and photographic evidence. There are undoubtedly many more damaged and destroyed trucks that left no digital evidence.
There are thousands of Russian trucks on the road in Ukraine every day, so hitting 700 of them in a month won't immediately strangle Russian logistics. But that accumulating destruction does strain Russian logistics—and terrify the truck drivers who are in the drone crosshairs. "Russian drivers post videos on a daily basis, showing how dangerous a ride in southern Ukraine is getting," Molin wrote.
What's remarkable is that the counterlogistics campaign hasn't faltered even as the Russians have adapted. Early on, Russian trucks mostly traveled alone and without protection, making them fairly easy picking for a bevy of Ukrainian middle-strike drone types including the Hornet, the B-2, the RAM 2X, the Chaklun, and various high-endurance first-person-view quadcopters.
The drones ride along Ukraine's overlapping command and control systems, which include Starlink satellite terminals (some dangling from balloons) as well as mesh radio networks. Many of the drones have built-in AI for autonomously detecting and homing in on trucks in the final seconds of flight.
Convoy operations
Reeling from the truck strikes, the Russians adapted this spring. Commanders began requiring all trucks to travel in convoys including mobile fire support groups, analysis group Tochnyi reported in May, citing Dmytro Putiata, a retired command post battle captain from the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces 20th Brigade "K2."
Trending Now
Today the Russian convoys have a standard structure, according to Molin. "Convoys usually gather three to five trucks and two to three air-defense trucks." Combined with radio jamming gear that's increasingly common on both the supply trucks and the gun trucks, that's seemingly a lot of protection.
But the drones target the gun trucks, too, peeling back the protection in order to expose the supply trucks to follow-on attacks. In that way, the Ukrainians have sustained their attacks on the supply trucks despite the increase in mobile air defense activity along the most important supply routes.
And it's going to get worse for the Russians as fall wears into winter. "Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare and the arrival of winter and more difficult conditions will not help," Molin wrote.
There will be less foliage on the trees lining the roads, and thus less cover from Ukrainian surveillance. Moreover, Molin pointed out, "it will be more difficult to go off-road" and avoid the big paved roads that are the main drone kill zones.
Russian logistics are under pressure, and that pressure is only increasing. Ultimately, the Ukrainians aim to starve Russian forces in Crimea. Strikes on cargo ships plying the Black Sea prevent the Russians from simply shifting the logistics off the coast. Meanwhile, strikes on overland logistics "may lead to substantial softening of front-line positions," Tochnyi noted in May.
Softening those front-line positions to the point of melting away could facilitate what Tochnyi described as "eventual breakthrough operations" in occupied southern Ukraine.
It's not inconceivable. Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps recently proved, by way of its successful Operation Vivaldi, that local Ukrainian counteroffensives are possible.
But that doesn't mean they're easy. To win, the 3rd Army Corps had to carefully husband its forces and meticulously prepare the battlefield under conditions of strict secrecy before attacking. That same kind of preparation is underway along the supply lines into Crimea, but it's unclear whether local Ukrainian forces have enough combat power in reserve to shift from defense to offense and exploit Russia's deepening supply woes.
At least not yet.

- Ukraine fired its first FP-7 ballistic missile in combat. Its maker says next version will do what Ukraine needed since 2022
- Ukraine keeps finding ways to replace its MiG-29s. It’s running out of MiG-29s to find

articles.title: Zelensky and Kiev mayor trade blame over Russian strikes
articles.body:
Zelensky and Kiev mayor trade blame over Russian strikes
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has slammed Kiev city authorities for an “almost complete failure” to protect the capital’s critical infrastructure from Russian attacks, escalating his longstanding feud with Mayor Vitaly Klitschko, who blames central government corruption.
In a social media post on Friday, Zelensky reported “extensive damage” to power grids following Russian strikes and criticized delays in strengthening infrastructure defenses across Ukraine, singling out Kiev for failing to take the necessary precautions.
His remarks came a day after Klitschko urged residents to consider temporarily leaving the capital, warning that the city was in “survival mode” as winter approaches.
In an interview with AFP on Thursday, Klitschko said Kiev was stockpiling food, drinking water and fuel. He urged residents with friends or relatives outside the capital to consider staying with them temporarily. However, he ruled out a full evacuation.
The mayor issued a similar warning in January, when a severe energy crisis left thousands of residential buildings without heating in freezing temperatures. The appeal sparked a public confrontation with Zelensky, who accused city authorities of failing to prepare adequately.
Speaking to AFP, Klitschko again blamed some of the shortcomings in Kiev’s winter preparations on Zelensky’s government. Rejecting accusations that city officials had fallen behind, he argued that “finding scapegoats won’t make people warmer.”
In a separate interview with Germany’s Bild published on Wednesday, Klitschko criticized corruption scandals linked to Zelensky’s administration, warning that wartime graft was “a real poison” for Ukraine.
The dispute comes amid escalating long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. Last week, Zelensky pledged to intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries, prompting Moscow to announce expanded strikes on Ukrainian military and defense-industrial facilities and supporting infrastructure, including in Kiev.
Moscow has said its strikes are in retaliation for Ukrainian drone and missile attacks on civilian targets inside Russia. According to Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik, 29 people, including two children, were killed in such attacks in the week ending October 4.
Klitschko warned that even extensive preparations might prove insufficient if the capital’s air defenses failed to repel further strikes.
Zelensky acknowledged a “big deficit” in air defenses on Thursday, appealing to Western backers for more interceptor missiles ahead of winter. Multiple media reports have linked shortages of Patriot interceptors in US and allied stockpiles to the US-Israeli war with Iran.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Fuel Plant, Oil Depot and Yandex Data Center as Moscow Claims 505 Drones Downed
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant producing fuel for Russian cruise missiles, an oil depot near the border region of Belgorod and infrastructure in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow overnight on Oct. 9, Russian officials and Ukrainian monitoring channels reported.
In the Tver region, which is situated between Moscow and St. Petersburg, drones hit the Redkino Experimental Plant and sparked a fire. The facility is the region’s largest chemical enterprise, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The facility manufactures Decylin-M, a specialized rocket fuel component used in Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, Kyiv Post sources within Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said in February, after the first strike on the enterprise.
Both missile types are among Russia’s primary long-range weapons used in strikes on Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure.
Regional Governor Vitaly Korolev said the fire had been extinguished and plant employees had been evacuated to a shelter. No workers were injured, he added.
Oil depot fire reported near Belgorod
In the Belgorod region, two people were killed and four others, including a child, were injured when shells struck private homes in the Belgorod district, the regional operational headquarters said.
Following the attack, NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at an oil depot north of Belgorod, Exilenova+ reported.
Trump May Leave 100,000 Ukrainians in US Immigration Limbo Rather Than Renew Protections
The depot supplies fuel to industrial and agricultural enterprises and gas stations across the region, according to its website.
Yandex data center damaged in Kaluga
A Yandex data center in Kaluga was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack overnight, marking the second consecutive day that the Russian technology company’s data centers have come under attack, RBC-Russia reported, citing the company’s press service.
Several modules at the Kaluga facility were completely disabled, potentially disrupting some services, Yandex said.
On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones struck another Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region, where servers host services used by the company and its clients. Operations at that facility were completely halted.
Kaluga Regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said nine people were injured in the overnight attacks across the region, five of whom were hospitalized.
Drones targeted four municipal districts and the regional capital, Kaluga. Shapsha said the drones struck what he described as the city’s “infrastructure.” Private homes were also damaged in two municipal districts and in Kaluga.
Shapsha said Russian air defenses intercepted 26 drones over the region.
Moscow claims 505 drones downed
Russia’s defense ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 505 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight over 19 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.
The ministry reported drone activity over Kaluga, Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Tula, Tver, Smolensk and Moscow regions, as well as Krasnodar Krai and Tatarstan.

articles.title: Fought against Ukraine, now claimed to be victims: Kenya’s plea for five men held by Ukraine
articles.body:
Kenya wants five of its citizens captured fighting for Russia in Ukraine to be treated as victims of human trafficking rather than prisoners of war, Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi told Kenyan lawmakers on 8 October, Bloomberg reported. Botswana is also seeking a citizen's return.
In 2025, Ukrainian ambassador Ivan Kholostenko called Russia's role in Africa neocolonialism. As Africa Corps troops prop up friendly regimes, the Kremlin is carrying out "a typical colonial practice of resource extraction," taking gold, diamonds, bauxite, and uranium, according to Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence. Russia also uses the continent as a recruiting ground for its war: nearly 500 Africans have died fighting for Russia, Ukraine says.
Five Kenyans in a Ukrainian camp
Kenya is negotiating to bring the five men home, and President William Ruto has raised the matter with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Mudavadi told the Senate. One has been held since November 2025, the others since March and April. The youngest is 23, Bloomberg reported. Kenya's honorary consul found them held in humane conditions at the Zakhid-1 camp, with access to medical care, the government said. Ukraine also holds the remains of four Kenyans.
Victims or fighters for hire
African governments say some of their citizens went to Russia for promised work as drivers, security guards, or cooks and were then forced into military service. The Kenyans "report having been recruited under false promises of employment," Mudavadi said.
"The circumstances of their recruitment and conscription are consistent with trafficking in persons," he said.
Ukraine's POW authority sees most foreign recruits differently. "The main motive for most of these mercenaries is financial gain," Dmytro Usov, secretary of Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, said in November 2025, while stressing that many had ended up in Russia's army through fraud or coercion.
Ghana negotiates Ukrainian drone deals as 1,780 Africans fight—and die—in Russia’s ranks
Ukraine holds that prisoners of war go home through exchanges, but Russia has never asked to trade for any foreign fighter except North Koreans, the headquarters said in May, adding it may consider other solutions if diplomats and lawyers find one.
Thousands of foreigners in Russia's ranks
Russia has recruited more than 28,000 foreigners from 135 countries, and more than 5,000 have been killed, a Ukrainian government website cited by Bloomberg says. Ukraine holds at least 213 foreign prisoners of war, not counting Russians and North Koreans, 37 of them African, according to documents Bloomberg saw. Russian dictator Vladimir Putin claimed on 3 September that people are "coming forward voluntarily and signing contracts."
Kenya's government counts 354 citizens linked to the war: 84 killed or missing, 34 hospitalized in Russia, and 62 repatriated. Petitioners told senators that 841 Kenyans remain unaccounted for. Mudavadi said his March visit to Moscow put Kenya on a Russian recruitment "stop list," with no new Kenyans enlisted since.
Some African governments take steps
In August, Botswana stopped eight citizens from joining the Russian military at airports in Botswana, South Africa, and Ethiopia, Bloomberg reported.
Ghana accused Russia of luring its citizens into the war the same month, after Kenya and South Africa. The European Parliament said in March that Russia strips African recruits of their documents. Ukraine, meanwhile, is drafting its first Africa strategy.

- Russia plans to open eight new cultural centers in Africa to court a loyal generation, HUR says

articles.title: Raytheon wins up to $6.3B to build more SM-3 interceptors
articles.body:
- Raytheon received a contract worth up to $6.3 billion over five years, plus two option years, to produce and sustain SM-3 Block IB interceptors.
- The interceptor was first used in combat in 2024, and production will take place mainly in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The U.S. Department of War and the Missile Defense Agency have awarded Raytheon a multiyear contract worth up to $6.3 billion to build and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors, the ship- and land-launched missiles the U.S. Navy uses to shoot down ballistic missiles in space.
The contract runs five years with two additional option years. It was issued as an undefinitized contract action, which lets Raytheon start work immediately while final terms and pricing are still being negotiated. Neither the Pentagon nor the company said how many interceptors the contract will buy or how quickly deliveries will begin. Production will take place mainly at Raytheon plants in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The SM-3 Block IB is built to destroy short- to intermediate-range ballistic missiles during the midcourse phase of flight, while they are outside the atmosphere, by hitting them directly rather than with an explosive warhead. It is launched from Aegis-equipped U.S. Navy destroyers and cruisers and from Aegis Ashore land sites, alongside the larger SM-3 Block IIA. The Block IB was first used in combat in April 2024, when U.S. Navy ships intercepted Iranian ballistic missiles fired at Israel, and it has been used again during this year’s war with Iran.
Raytheon said the award supports urgent replenishment of missile defense stocks that have been drawn down in combat.
“This award underscores Raytheon’s commitment to increasing production of critical munitions, ensuring our customers have the defensive capabilities they need, when they need them,” said Raytheon President Phil Jasper. “SM-3 Block IB has proven its relevance in combat and this contract helps ensure we can replenish inventories and keep pace with the evolving threats the U.S. Navy, MDA and their partners face around the world.”
The Pentagon said the multiyear deal is meant to give industry the production certainty to invest in assembly lines, solid rocket motor suppliers and smaller domestic subcontractors, where shortages have limited how fast interceptors can be built.
“Our warfighters must never face a fair fight, and the SM-3 Blk IB has proven its operational superiority to dominate any adversary across the globe,” said Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of war for acquisition and sustainment. “This contract provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required to dominate the battle space.”
The award is the latest under five framework agreements Raytheon signed with the Department of War in February, covering expanded production of Tomahawk cruise missiles, AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, SM-3 Block IB, SM-3 Block IIA and SM-6 under deals of up to seven years. Last week, Raytheon received a contract worth up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 production under the same framework.
The SM-3 Block IB line had slowed before the current buildup. In March, the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon about $267 million for 23 more Block IB interceptors to restart production, bringing that order to 78 missiles, along with an $8.41 billion increase to the ceiling of a contract for SM-3 sustainment and engineering support.

articles.title: Zelensky ‘doesn’t give a damn’ about Ukrainians – Russian envoy
articles.body:
Zelensky ‘doesn’t give a damn’ about Ukrainians – Russian envoy
Vladimir Zelensky’s continued attempts to target Moscow despite harsh retaliation against Ukraine’s military-related infrastructure prove that he doesn’t care about the well-being of his country’s people, Russia’s ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Dmitry Polyansky, has said.
Moscow Region came under a major aerial attack on Tuesday night, with Ukraine firing 650 drones towards the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said. Despite most of the UAVs being shot down by air defenses, the raid resulted in the death of two people. Another civilian was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the region on Thursday, according to Governor Andrey Vorobyev.
During his speech at an OSCE session in the Austrian capital, Vienna, on Thursday, Polyansky said that Zelensky “still harbors hopes of inflicting at least some noticeable damage on Moscow” in order to present this to the West as “proof that Ukraine is still capable of carrying out military operations that are painful” for Russia.
“At the same time, the head of the Kiev regime never tires of threatening Russia with escalation – something he is incapable of actually delivering – only to then complain about large-scale strikes by Russia,” he said, as cited by TASS.
Zelensky should remember the proverb that “people who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones,” the envoy noted.
According to Polyansky, Russian retaliatory strikes on facilities supporting Kiev’s war machine are “many times more powerful” than those attempted by Ukrainian forces. Because of those attacks, Ukraine is “losing the last remnants of its industry and infrastructure,” while also teetering on the brink of a “total energy and transport collapse” ahead of winter, he added.
Zelensky, however, “doesn’t give a damn about his citizens. His only concern is siphoning more money out of the country into the corruption system of his creation,” Polyansky said.
Ukraine has been rocked by a series of high-profile corruption scandals since last year, with the largest centering on a $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Zelensky. Other recent graft probes have targeted former Ukrainian ministers, prosecutors, diplomats, and senior officials.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Zelensky said he had ordered the Ukrainian military to double the number of attacks deep inside Russia, particularly against the country’s oil refining facilities.
The Russian Defense Ministry responded by announcing that “following Zelensky’s statement, the strikes... on military and military-industrial facilities… in Kiev and other regions of Ukraine will be intensified.” The ministry maintains that it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Ground Robots Rescued 45 Soldiers Under Fire, Commander Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s ground robots rescued 45 soldiers from under Russian fire and transported more than 41 tons of supplies to frontline positions during the summer of 2026, according to the Artan special unit under Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
Artan commander Col. Viktor Torkotiuk, call sign Titan, said crews operating the unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) worked continuously along the front, according to RBC-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
During the summer campaign, the platforms covered a combined distance of approximately 4,258 kilometers (2,646 miles), with tasks ranging from supporting frontline logistics to evacuating wounded Ukrainian troops and transporting captured Russian soldiers.
Robots enter areas too dangerous for vehicles
The ground platforms allowed Ukrainian forces to evacuate wounded troops from exposed positions without sending additional personnel or conventional vehicles into areas monitored by Russian drones.
Torkotiuk said the drones help free up valuable resources.
“Technology is transforming the combat capabilities of units on the front line,” Torkotiuk said. “Innovative logistics frees up capabilities and forces for active operations and offensive actions,” he added.
The unit did not specify how many vehicles took part in the missions, how many individual journeys they completed, or which ground-robot models they used.
Ground robotic systems vary in size and configuration. Some transport ammunition, food and other supplies, while others can carry wounded soldiers, conduct reconnaissance, clear mines or operate mounted weapons.
Russia Steps Up Production of Improved Su-34 ‘Fullback’ Bombers
Ukrainian troops have said such platforms are particularly useful inside the so-called kill zone, where ordinary evacuation vehicles can quickly be detected and targeted by surveillance and attack drones.
Frontline soldiers have previously told Kyiv Post that robots are not replacing troops but are increasingly performing the most dangerous logistical and medical evacuation missions.
Artan operates in Zaporizhzhia and near Lyman
Artan said its main area of operations is currently the Zaporizhzhia front in southern Ukraine, a region where over 70 percent is under Russian occupation, most of which since 2022.
The unit also participated in one stage of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi near Lyman in eastern Ukraine during the spring and summer campaign. The operation recovered at least 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory and disrupted Russian attempts to advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Analysts suggest the operation has reversed Russian gains made in 2026 and thwarted Moscow’s goal to capture eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
The HUR special operations unit was formed on June 1, 2022. Its personnel have fought in some of the war’s most contested areas and participated in land and Black Sea operations, including the 2023 campaign that helped open the road to Klishchiivka and create an escape route for Ukrainian forces encircled by the Russians in the Donetsk region’s Bakhmut.
Ukraine expands its robotic army
Ukraine is rapidly increasing its use of ground robots to reduce the number of soldiers exposed during supply runs and casualty evacuations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky set a target to provide the military with at least 50,000 ground robotic systems by 2026.
The systems are becoming a regular part of frontline operations as Ukraine seeks to compensate for personnel shortages and adapt to a battlefield where drones can detect and attack conventional vehicles several kilometers behind the contact line.

articles.title: Trump rules out Iran strikes as Pentagon draws up plans
articles.body:
(Getty Images)
The Pentagon has drawn up plans for an intensive three-day military campaign against Iran, the U.S. media reported on Oct. 8, even as President Donald Trump said Washington will not launch an attack before the Nov. 3 elections.
The U.S. military, acting on Trump’s orders, has developed options to strike Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, energy facilities and other military sites, The Times reported, citing U.S. officials.
Senior national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed the plans at Camp David last week, with the options centering on a short, intensive campaign lasting about three days, according to people briefed on the proposal.
The strikes would focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which has been rebuilt by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) since the early phase of the war, the newspaper said.
Other potential targets include Iranian energy facilities as well as IRGC command posts and headquarters.
Axios separately reported that the Pentagon ordered the US Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran.
The directive did not set a date for strikes and Trump had not made a final decision, Axios said, adding that any renewed major combat operations were expected to include large-scale bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets.
The military preparations come as Trump said on Oct. 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while pointing to ongoing diplomatic efforts.
“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” he wrote.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Washington and Tehran were having “productive discussions.”
Trump’s announcement on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to the elections.
The New York Times also reported that Trump has repeatedly declined proposals in recent months to resume major combat operations against Iran, despite ordering the Pentagon to prepare new options.
Three U.S. aircraft carriers are expected to be in the Middle East in the coming weeks as part of the major military buildup, according to the newspaper.

articles.title: Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed, Rogers spar over Iran, Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed and Rogers spar over Iran and Israel
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers traded barbs on Thursday over Iran and Israel during their first televised debate in the race for Michigan’s open Senate seat, ahead of November’s US midterm elections.
Held in Grand Rapids, Michigan, the debate opened with both candidates being asked whether they would support a pause on the federal petrol tax amid rising fuel prices linked to the war with Iran.
Fuel prices have surged since US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February triggered the conflict, adding to concerns over the cost of living among American voters.
Both candidates backed a pause on the federal petrol tax before turning to their respective positions on the war.
Rogers, who initially supported the US offensive against Iran, has since called for the months-long conflict to end.
The Republican Senate candidate reiterated that position during the debate, as did El-Sayed, who has repeatedly criticised the Trump administration over its handling of the war.
The Democrat also blamed the administration for Iran’s decision to close the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.
“This is what happens when you start wars you never should be fighting,” El-Sayed said.
“We literally taught the Iranian regime that they have a choke on the Strait of Hormuz, and now we’re living in that reality.”
Although Rogers agreed that “we need [the war] to come to an end”, he defended the military campaign, arguing that US attacks had set Iran’s uranium enrichment programme back by “twenty years”.
His remarks echoed claims by the Trump administration that military action was necessary to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied US and Israeli accusations that it is seeking to develop nuclear weapons.
The Islamic Republic maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful, while insisting that it will not compromise on its civilian nuclear activities or make structural concessions without the lifting of US economic sanctions.
El-Sayed criticised Rogers for his support of the war and for defending the Trump administration, accusing him of changing his position for political reasons rather than out of concern for Americans’ financial circumstances.
"The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers,” El-Sayed said.
He added moments later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”
El-Sayed and Rogers clash over Israel
During the debate, El-Sayed faced questions over his criticism of Israel’s genocidal military campaign in Gaza, following his recent refusal to say whether he considers Israel or Iran a greater threat to the US in an interview with US cable news network NewsNation.
The candidates hold opposing positions on US military assistance to Israel, which has received more US foreign aid cumulatively than any other country since the Second World War.
Rogers reaffirmed his support for continued US aid to Israel, while El-Sayed called for an end to military assistance, arguing that American taxpayers’ money should instead be directed towards domestic priorities such as education and healthcare.
“He wants unconditional support for a foreign government,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “I want unconditional support for kids in our schools, unconditional support for our healthcare, childcare.”
The Democrat also blamed Israel for drawing the US into military action against Iran.
“I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in war with Iran,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers, meanwhile, argued that Israel had “the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood”, reiterating his support for the country.
“Is there anything Israel could do that would lose your support?” debate moderator Rick Albin asked.
“Listen, if they’re talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support,” Rogers replied.
Rogers targets El-Sayed over Muslim identity
Beyond their disagreements over foreign policy, the candidates repeatedly traded personal insults.
El-Sayed described his Republican rival as “weak”, “cowardly” and a “sock puppet for the Trump administration”. Rogers, in turn, called his opponent a “glitchy AI chatbot” who was running a “con” and would “say anything to win”.
The pair also challenged each other over campaign donations and their personal finances.
El-Sayed lambasted Rogers over a waterfront property he owns in Florida, while Rogers pointed to a rental property owned by El-Sayed’s wife in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Albin, the candidates continued arguing even when the cameras were off. The moderator repeatedly urged them to maintain order, telling them to “work with me” and adding: “I appreciate your passion, but please, let's try to keep this orderly.”
The debate also covered the trade dispute with Canada, immigration, healthcare, and the cost of living.
However, some of Rogers’ attacks arguably fixated on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and alleged associations with extremist groups.
El-Sayed has repeatedly faced Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, with Trump leading attacks on the Democrat, including labelling him as an “extremist, terrorist sympathizer”.
Trump also claimed his history “goes back to the days of the Jihad” in a post on Truth Social.
During the debate, a discussion about healthcare led Rogers to claim that El-Sayed had “taken money from individuals on his campaign who openly support Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda”.
The former US congressman also challenged El-Sayed over his opposition to surveillance cameras operated by Flock Safety, arguing that the technology had helped apprehend people suspected of terrorism.
Rogers then suggested that El-Sayed’s concerns about the cameras warranted further scrutiny.
“Why would that bother you?” Rogers asked. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the terrorism watch list...”
El-Sayed interrupted, challenging Rogers to make explicit the implication he appeared to be suggesting.
“Are you going to go ahead and say that I’m a – go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing about it the whole time. Just say it. Just say it. Go ahead and say it.”
The exchange comes amid repeated attacks on El-Sayed’s Arab and Muslim identity during his campaign, highlighting wider concerns about Islamophobia directed at Muslim and Arab candidates in US politics.
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
Michigan Senate race could shape control of Congress
A CBS News poll published earlier this week showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 45.6 per cent to 41.4 per cent, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
The race is among those expected to help determine which party controls the Senate following the midterm elections.
The elections will shape the final two years of Trump’s presidential term, with Republicans facing the prospect of losing their current hold on Congress amid the president’s declining popularity and the fallout from the war on Iran.
Trump himself has been holding numerous rallies to potentially reverse the party’s political fortunes.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Strike Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant, a Rocket Fuel Component Manufacturer
articles.body:
Strike drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant in Russia’s Tver region overnight on October 9. The facility manufactures chemical products used by Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on this.
Footage published online shows strike drones flying overhead, followed by explosions and a fire near the plant. Local residents also reported Russian air defense activity in the area.
Tver region governor Vitaliy Korolyov confirmed that a fire broke out at the plant in the settlement of Redkino following a drone attack. According to him, the plant’s employees were evacuated to a shelter in time, and no one was injured. The fire has since been extinguished.
The facility is one of the major chemical industrial sites in the Tver region.
The plant produces specialty chemicals in small batches and manufactures more than 40 types of products for the aviation, aerospace, and other industries.
Its products include ferrocene derivatives, which are used as combustion catalysts in solid-propellant rocket engines, as well as specialty materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives.
According to the Security Service of Ukraine, the plant manufactures components for the special fuel Decilin-M, used in Russia’s Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
In September 2025, the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on the facility. The British government cited its activities in Russia’s strategically important defense and chemical sectors as the basis for the restrictions.
Militarnyi previously reported that the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant was targeted twice by strike drones in a single night on June 27, 2024.
At the time, Russian sources reported that plant personnel had been evacuated, while Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that four drones had been intercepted over the Tver region.
The plant was also targeted in September 2023 and, according to monitoring channels, in February 2026.

articles.title: NATO asks Russia ‘not to worry’ despite earlier threats
articles.body:
NATO asks Russia ‘not to worry’ about nuclear drills
NATO has asked Moscow “not to worry” about the US-led military bloc’s upcoming nuclear warfare drills, despite weeks of escalated war rhetoric from its member states, which are ostensibly preparing their populations for a war with Russia.
NATO’s forces will practice responding to launch orders, flying mock nuclear delivery sorties, and maintaining communications under the stress of nuclear war during its ‘Steadfast Noon’ exercises from October 13 to 23. The drill will involve 17 of the bloc’s 32 member states and will not involve live nuclear weapons.
This year alone, bloc forces have run three separate exercises on the borders of the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, after which Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski suggested a further buildup of NATO forces in the area in order to keep Moscow “uncertain of what we will do.”
The Kremlin issued a stern warning in response, stating that Russia is “ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad.”
The message apparently fell on deaf ears. On Wednesday, Estonia’s foreign minister claimed that NATO possessed the ability to close the Baltic Sea “within hours,” strangling Russia’s economic “lifeline” and creating an “existential” crisis for the country. Last week, Swedish Air Warfare Centre chief Colonel Carl Bergqvist said his country’s warplanes were ready to attack targets deep inside Russian territory in the event of a conflict with Moscow.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and European governments insisted in recent weeks that Russia is waging a “hybrid war” against the West. The accusations are by their nature unprovable, and have been described by analyst Thomas Fazi as a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, in which “Europeans are being subjected to a sustained campaign of cognitive or psychological warfare aimed at conditioning them to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia.”
NATO’s nuclear policy director, Nassima Barrows, told Politico on Thursday that the fact that the drills are held every year should serve as “a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry.”
Despite Burrows’ reassurances, and NATO’s description of Steadfast Noon as “not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country,” some of the bloc’s leaders evidently view their nuclear weapons as a tool with which to threaten Russia. After watching the test-launch of France’s latest nuclear-capable ballistic missile on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron released a video of the test, describing it as “a clear message…for wherever it must be received.”
Russia read the message “loud and clear,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded, adding that Russia will take “all necessary measures” to protect its national security.
During his speech at a session of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Vienna on Thursday, Russian envoy Dmitry Polyansky reiterated that Moscow “threatens no one and has no intention of attacking anyone.”
At the same time, however, the country “cannot ignore the development of plans by NATO for a direct military clash with Russia, nor the bloc’s simulation of scenarios involving a military-political blockade of Kaliningrad Region,” he stressed.
“Our response to any unfriendly moves will be swift,” Polyansky said, urging NATO not to test Russia’s patience or push the European continent “toward the point of no return.”

articles.title: Ukraine, Europe, US to meet in Miami for talks on ending war
articles.body:
Ukraine, Europe, US officials to meet for talks to end war
October 9, 2026
Ukrainian and European officials are set to meet US President Donald Trump's envoys in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" to end Russia's war in Ukraine.
Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the meeting on Thursday evening, after a Russian attack on buses killed 30 civilians in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.
Before the strikes in Kramatorsk, a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment block in the northern Chernihiv region, killing 22 Ukrainians, including five children.
More than 70 people have been killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine in the past two days, Zelenskyy said.
What did Zelenskyy say about the Miami meeting?
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, and other top officials, including Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia, will also attend, the Ukrainian president said.
"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region", one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.
"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.
Zelenskyy blames US for inaction
Amid rising civilian casualties and fears of further escalation, Zelenskyy urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service, which would help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I've said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse the US of being unwilling to pressure Russia into negotiations, adding that enabling Starlink would cost Washington nothing.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
Ukraine president rejects Rubio claim that war is deadlocked
Zelenskyy was responding to remarks on Wednesday from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the war in Ukraine was at a stalemate.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that he agreed with Rubio's assessment, adding that he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskyy said, countering the US narrative. "We are not a diplomatic dead end," he said.
Zelenskyy also called for tougher sanctions to cripple the Russian economy, a point Ukrainian officials are expected to press US envoys on at the meeting.

articles.title: Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
articles.body:
This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: October 9, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
Since September 21, we added more than 17,000 individuals to our list of Russian losses. As we explained in previous updates, this is unrelated to the current situation at the front: we process reports of missing persons and confirm the deaths of the missing via official state registries.
Additionally, for this update, we have confirmed the deaths of 20 officers during the massive missile strike on Donetsk on August 26. Read the report here:
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By October 9, 2026, the death of 7,833 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 259,800 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 261,300 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.
