articles.title: Zelenskyy revealed which drones the Defense Forces used to strike Russian oil refineries: modified FP-1s and An-196 RS
articles.body:
Zelenskyy revealed which drones the Defense Forces used to strike Russian oil refineries: modified FP-1s and An-196 RS
Kyiv • UNN
President Zelenskyy reported that Russia’s Omsk Oil Refinery was hit by FP-6 drones (modified FP-1s), while the Ukhta Oil Refinery was struck by An-196 RS unmanned aerial vehicles.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said exactly what weapons the Defense Forces used to strike Russian oil refineries. According to him, the Omsk Refinery was attacked by FP-6 drones (modified FP-1 drones). An-196 RS unmanned aerial vehicles (part of the family of Ukrainian long-range "Liutyi" drones) were used to strike the Ukhta Refinery, UNN reports.
Omsk Refinery is Russia's largest oil refinery, with a capacity of about 22 million tonnes of oil per year. It is located approximately 2,500 km from the Ukrainian border in Russia's Omsk region. The facility is owned by the Russian company "Gazprom Neft." It produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, lubricants, and other petroleum products.
Another target of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Ukhta Refinery, is located 1,900 km from the Ukrainian border in the Komi Republic. The facility is owned by the Russian company "Lukoil" and processes about 4.2 million tonnes of oil per year. The refinery produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and other petroleum products.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, both facilities are involved in supplying the Russian army.
The president also confirmed the strike on another Russian data center, calling it a mirror response to Russia's strikes on Ukraine. The defense company Fire Point, whose drones were used by the Defense Forces to hit the target, said that it was the largest data center of the Russian company "Yandex" — "Yandex DC Kaluga." It is located in the Grabtsevo industrial park in Russia's Kaluga region.
Photo source: @firepointofficial
The facility's designed capacity is 63 MW. According to the Ukrainian defense company, several modules of the data center were completely disabled as a result of the strikes.
As of 2026, "Yandex" has five large data centers, two of which have been attacked by the Defense Forces of Ukraine over the past two days. On October 8, Ukrainian drones struck the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region. Following the strike, disruptions to the operation of a number of online services were recorded in Russia.
Recall
On October 8, the Defense Forces struck the "Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat" oil refinery complex in Bashkortostan with FP-1 drones. The drones traveled more than 1,300 km to carry out the attack.
The capacity of the Salavat complex is up to 10 million tonnes of hydrocarbon feedstock per year. According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the facility is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian army.

articles.title: Zelenskyy discusses accelerating licensing for Patriot missile production with US congressmen
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Kyiv with a U.S. Congressional delegation to discuss the implementation of the late Senator Lindsey Graham's bill, as well as accelerating the licensing process for the production of Patriot missiles.
"I am grateful to the U.S. congressional delegation – Roger Wicker, Kevin Cramer, Marc Veasey and Dan Crenshaw – for standing with our people today amid virtually nonstop Russian attacks. Russia is not getting what it wanted on the battlefield and is trying to compensate for this by escalating the conflict," Zelenskyy said on his Telegram channel on Friday following the meeting.
According to him, an air raid alert remained in effect throughout the entire meeting in the capital due to the threat of "suicide" drones.
The president said that since the beginning of the month, the Russians have damaged two schools in Kyiv with such drones and have struck bridges, power facilities, and other critical infrastructure.
"We can only defend ourselves against this terror by working together, and we discussed how the United States can help save lives. Of course, we expect the Lindsey Graham Act to be enacted. This is a matter of political will, and it is now important to show leadership and completely cut off financial flows to the Russian war machine. We also discussed other necessary steps, including accelerating the licensing of Patriot missile production. Ukraine is ready not only to produce ballistic interceptors for itself but also to strengthen the United States and its allies through joint production," he said.
Zelenskyy thanked the United States for its unwavering support.

articles.title: Ukrainian journalists say they were detained “like terrorists”: prosecutor says suspicion unsubstantiated
articles.body:
Austrian police detained Ukrainian investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko in Vienna yesterday, on 8 October. Both were later released, but the circumstances of their detention remain unclear, and the prosecutor’s office said suspicion against them had not been substantiated so far.
The detention lasted more than 12 hours, the first time Tkach had been held that long while on a reporting assignment abroad. The case unfolded alongside a separate Austrian espionage investigation involving two men suspected of working for Ukraine’s military intelligence. Authorities have not said whether the cases are connected.
Tkach describes detention
In a video published by Ukrainska Pravda, Tkach said seven people wearing masks and carrying weapons approached their car at a traffic light about 3–5 kilometers from central Vienna, broke its windows, and pointed weapons at them.
He said the people did not identify themselves or explain their actions. The journalists were pulled from the car, forced face down onto the road, searched, and had their hands taped behind their backs, according to Tkach. He said he initially thought they were being kidnapped because he did not see identification or have time to notice police markings. He realized they were police only after seeing police vehicles.
“As I felt it, they detained us like terrorists,” Tkach said.
He added that people shouted and pointed weapons, and there was no communication. He said one person put a knee on his neck and shouted at him to be quiet. He also saw glass from the broken window fly into Bondarenko’s face.
In a second report, Ukrainska Pravda said Tkach’s account of a document presented to him listed three allegations: espionage in the interests of Ukrainian military intelligence, participation in a criminal organization, and, as far as he remembered, causing harm to Austria. He said investigators did not explain the evidence behind the allegations.
Vienna prosecutor’s office spokesperson Nina Bussek told the Austrian Press Agency (APA) that suspicion against the two journalists had arisen during other investigations but had not been substantiated. She said it currently appeared that the suspicion was not holding up. Austrian officials have not publicly addressed Tkach’s account of the force used.
Diplomatic response and calls for an investigation
Tkach and Bondarenko were in Vienna on an assignment to find Ruslan Kravchenko, Ukraine’s former prosecutor general, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Kravchenko was dismissed on 15 September amid an investigation by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office into alleged protection of fraudulent call centers. He denied involvement. Der Standard reported that it remained unclear whether the journalists’ detention was connected to their reporting on him.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed Tkach’s release and said the Ukrainian consul had requested access to him, according to NV. Musaieva said Bondarenko had been injured and hospitalized.
A statement signed by Ukrainian media and civil society organizations, including Euromaidan Press, called for an immediate, transparent, and independent investigation of law enforcement’s actions. The signatories also demanded an independent review of the force used, the return of seized equipment, and necessary medical and legal assistance.
Separate espionage investigation
Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner confirmed the arrests of four Ukrainians, according to ORF. The two men detained on 5 October were placed in pretrial detention until 21 October on suspicion of secret intelligence activity against Austria. APA reported that they were suspected employees of Ukraine’s military intelligence service. Both deny the allegations.

articles.title: Over 100 groups condemn Israeli actions during so-called 'truce'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'There is no ceasefire’: Over 100 organisations condemn so called Gaza 'truce'
Exactly one year after a ceasefire was reached in Gaza, over 100 humanitarian, human rights, and other civil society organisations have highlighted Israel's continued attacks on the enclave, stating that the truce has been "meaningless".
Organisations including Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), ActionAid and Save the Children were among those denouncing Israel’s actions since the truce was agreed in October 2025.
At least 1,471 Palestinians have been killed since then, with daily demolitions carried out and civilians targeted.
“What we see on the ground is that the ceasefire exists in name only. A ceasefire is absolutely meaningless when civilians, including children, are being killed every single day,” Alexandra Saieh, Head of Policy and Global Influencing at Save the Children, told The New Arab.
"The reality is, there is no ceasefire."
Saieh said they see Israeli airstrikes, shooting, and drone attacks that are killing children and other civilians every single day in the enclave.
“The ceasefire has left Palestinians in Gaza teetering at the edge of survival,” she noted.
The organisations asserted that “the killing and deprivation in the enclave must not be normalised under the cover of a ceasefire agreement”, also noting the Israeli military has moved the its 'Yellow Line' further into Gaza, restricting the movement of Palestinians and dividing the enclave further.
“There was never a real ceasefire in Gaza. The genocide is not over: every day Palestinians are forced to survive in conditions that can only be described as unliveable,” Riham Jafari, advocacy and communications coordinator at ActionAid Palestine told The New Arab.
Jafari explains that instead of a truce, the Israeli army has “continued to kill and injure hundreds of people, pursuing its strategy of death, expulsion and colonial domination”, noting the unprecedented levels of violence in the occupied West Bank.
“The world must not normalise what is happening in Gaza. The impunity must end. There must be full accountability and justice for all atrocities that have been committed.”
The terms of the October ceasefire said that Israel was meant to withdraw from major cities in the enclave, Palestinian prisoners were to be freed, and large amounts of humanitarian aid were to enter the enclave daily through crossings; however, Israel has continued to target Palestinians with daily attacks and frequent strikes.
Israel also continues to prevent vital aid, including medicine, from entering the Strip, putting the thousands of Palestinians' lives at risk.
“There are still severe shortages of the most basic things in hospitals here, including IV fluids, anaesthetic medicines, and surgical consumables, which can directly affect whether we can provide surgical services,” Sally Saleh, MAP’s Head of Emergency in Gaza, told The New Arab.
Saleh notes there are also heavy restrictions on medical items classified by Israel as “dual use”, including laboratory equipment, reagent components for laboratory machines, imaging equipment, neonatal intensive care units and ventilators.
Activists say Israel regularly uses the "dual use" classification, alleging that it could be used for attacks or military purposes, as a way to prevent aid from entering Gaza and putting a stop to the recovery and reconstruction process.
“From a health perspective, these restrictions can have very dire consequences, such as delays in diagnosis, disease surveillance, and treatment,” Saleh notes.
Three years since the outbreak of the genocidal war, Palestinians have faced little reprieve, forced to live in tents for shelter as over 80 percent of structures across the enclave have been damaged.
Despite promises of peace and reconstruction, with multiple agencies declaring Israel’s war a genocide, Gazans are still waiting for the war to be officially over.
“The reconstruction and rebuilding of Gaza should not be conditioned on political or security outcomes,” Saieh asserts.
“Palestinians in Gaza have the right to rebuild their homes and to recover, and they have just not been allowed to do that.”

articles.title: Trump says Witkoff 'doing very well' in Iran talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump says Witkoff 'doing very well' in Iran talks
US President Donald Trump said US envoy Steve Witkoff is "doing very well" in talks with Iran, as the president once again predicted that the months-long war will end "very soon".
Speaking at a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, on Wednesday, Trump said Witkoff was making progress in negotiations with Iran but suggested that reaching a deal was not his preferred outcome.
"He's working on the Iran deal and doing very well. I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," Trump said.
"They will never have a nuclear weapon," he added.
The US president also said he expects the war with Iran to end soon.
"That war ends - it's going to be very soon. It's got to be very soon," Trump said, describing Iran as "a failed nation."
Despite expressing initial reluctance to strike a deal with Tehran, Trump said in a Thursday post on Truth Social that the US is continually engaged in productive discussions with Iran.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote.
He added that the US blockade of Iranian ports remained in place and that oil was continuing to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, amid discussions on reopening the vital global energy shipping route.
"We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," Trump said.
The statement comes amid GOP concerns that any escalation in the US-Iran conflict ahead of the November midterm elections could put Trump's Republican Party at risk of losing control of both houses of Congress.
However, recent reports said the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop military options for potential strikes on Iranian targets before 3 November.
Trump officials were also debating the possible scale and targets of any strikes, as well as whether the president would ultimately authorise military action, according to The Atlantic.
Several of Trump's advisers reportedly believed the timing would be more appropriate after the elections, the publication reported.
Axios also reported that the Pentagon had instructed US Central Command (CENTCOM) to prepare for a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran.
Citing US officials, the report said the directive did not specify a date for any potential military action.
The latest developments come as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict remain uncertain.
Washington has emphasised restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities as a key condition for a lasting agreement.
